body:
What is digital identity?

When a person applies for a scholarship, opens an online bank account or accesses a government service, the organisation may need to establish who that person is. In a physical setting, identity may be checked using documents and records. In a digital setting, information stored or verified electronically performs a similar function.

Digital identity is a collection of electronically recorded attributes and identifiers that can be used to distinguish an individual and, where necessary, establish that the individual is the person they claim to be.

An identity may contain attributes such as name, date of birth and address. It may also be associated with an identifier, such as an account number or an Aadhaar number. Different systems require different levels of identity assurance. A public information website may allow access without establishing a visitor's real-world identity, while a service that transfers money to an eligible beneficiary may require more reliable identification.

Identifiers are not necessarily proof of identity

An identifier is a value used to distinguish a person, record or account within a particular system. Examples include a student registration number, employee ID, username, mobile number and Aadhaar number. An identifier may be unique within one institution without being unique across the country.

Knowing a person's identifier does not establish that the person using it is its rightful holder. For example, knowing someone's email address does not mean that the email account belongs to the person entering it. Similarly, entering an Aadhaar number is not, by itself, the same as successfully completing Aadhaar authentication.

Four related but different processes

ProcessMeaningExample
IdentificationDetermining which person or record is involved.Locating a student's record using a registration number.
Identity proofingEstablishing that a claimed identity corresponds to a real person using suitable evidence.Checking identity documents during enrolment.
AuthenticationChecking whether someone attempting access is the legitimate holder of an identity or account.Verifying a password, OTP or biometric characteristic.
AuthorizationDeciding what an authenticated person is permitted to access or do.Allowing a student to view their own marks but not another student's marks.

Know Your Customer (KYC) refers to procedures used by an organisation, particularly in regulated financial services, to establish and verify a customer's identity and satisfy applicable requirements. KYC is not simply another name for entering a password.

How the processes fit together

Consider an online scholarship portal. At registration, the applicant supplies identity details and any required evidence. The portal creates or associates an account with the applicant. During a later visit, the applicant authenticates using the permitted method. Once the applicant is authenticated, the portal allows only the functions appropriate to that account. Eligibility for a scholarship is a further decision based on applicable scheme conditions; successful login does not itself establish eligibility.

A genuine identity, a successful login and eligibility for a government benefit are 3 separate matters. A person may successfully authenticate but still be ineligible for a particular scheme.

Digital identity is useful because the same verified information may support multiple interactions, subject to applicable rules and privacy safeguards. However, the benefits depend on accurate records, secure authentication and accessible alternatives for people who cannot use a particular technology.

Prelims focus

  • An identifier distinguishes a person or account; it is not necessarily a secret.
  • Identity proofing establishes a claimed identity using evidence.
  • Authentication checks whether the claimant is the legitimate account or identity holder.
  • Authorization determines the actions or resources permitted after authentication.
  • KYC concerns identity verification and applicable customer-identification requirements.
  • Trap: Successful authentication does not automatically establish entitlement to a subsidy or service.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 10, 'Transport and Communication,' printed pp. 122–123; National Institute of Standards and Technology, Digital Identity Guidelines, SP 800-63-4, 2025, digital identity model and identity proofing; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: Digital Identity: Meaning, Identifiers and the Stages of Establishing Identity

body:
Authentication establishes that the claimant is legitimate

A digital service needs more than a username to decide whether a person should receive access. It must check suitable evidence that the person attempting to log in controls the account or identity being claimed. This process is called authentication.

Authentication methods are commonly classified according to the type of evidence they use. The important distinction is between what a person knows, what a person possesses and what a person is.

The 3 authentication factors

FactorMeaningExamplesMain limitation
KnowledgeSomething the person knows.Password, PIN.It may be guessed, stolen or disclosed.
PossessionSomething the person controls or possesses.Registered phone, security token, authentication device.The device may be lost, stolen or compromised.
InherenceSomething related to the person's physical or behavioural characteristics.Fingerprint, iris pattern, face.Matching may fail, and biometric information cannot be changed like a password.

A PIN means Personal Identification Number. Although a PIN consists of digits, it is normally a knowledge factor because the legitimate user is expected to know it. An OTP means One-Time Password. It is intended for limited use, often during a short validity period. An OTP delivered to a registered device can provide evidence of possession of that device or communication channel.

Whether an OTP supplies a separate authentication factor depends on the complete authentication process. Simply asking for 2 passwords does not create 2 different factor categories.

Single-factor and multi-factor authentication

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is authentication that uses at least 2 distinct authentication factors. When exactly 2 factors are used, the method is commonly called two-factor authentication (2FA).

A password followed by an OTP received through a separately controlled registered phone is a familiar example of 2-factor authentication. A password followed by another memorised security answer still relies on knowledge and does not become multi-factor merely because 2 questions are asked.

A phone or other device may also use a PIN or biometric characteristic to activate a locally held authenticator. The important requirement is the combination of distinct factors, not the appearance of 2 screens or 2 successive steps.

Why MFA improves security

If an attacker learns a password, MFA can require additional evidence before granting access. This reduces dependence on a single secret. It does not make an account completely secure. Criminals may deceive users into revealing OTPs, compromise devices or exploit weak account-recovery procedures.

Phishing and OTP fraud

Phishing is an attempt to trick someone into disclosing sensitive information or taking an unsafe action, often through a fraudulent message or website. An OTP remains confidential even when a message claims to be from a bank or government office. A legitimate login process should be initiated through the appropriate service rather than through an unverified link.

A well-designed authentication system also needs a safe recovery method. If a person loses a phone, forgetting or replacing the registered authentication method should not permanently exclude them from an essential service. Recovery must be secure enough to prevent impersonation while remaining accessible to legitimate users.

Authentication factor refers to the category of evidence. Authentication step refers to an action in a process. Multiple steps can use the same factor.

Prelims focus

  • Password and PIN are knowledge factors.
  • A controlled authentication device is a possession factor.
  • Fingerprint, iris and face are biometric or inherence factors.
  • MFA combines at least 2 distinct factor categories.
  • An OTP is designed for limited use and should not be shared.
  • Trap: Password plus another password is not multi-factor authentication.

[Sources: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, SP 800-63B-4, 2025, authenticator types and multi-factor authenticators; NIST, Digital Identity Guidelines, SP 800-63-4, 2025, glossary; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: Authentication Methods and Multi-Factor Authentication

body:
Why biological characteristics can be used for identity

A biometric system uses measurable characteristics of a person to support identification or authentication. Fingerprint patterns, iris patterns and facial characteristics are common examples. These characteristics can help distinguish people because they differ between individuals and can be compared with previously recorded reference information.

Biometric matching is not the same as reading a person's name from a document. A system captures a biometric sample, processes relevant features and compares them with stored reference information. The comparison produces a result according to the system's matching criteria.

Biometrics can reduce reliance on memorised passwords or physical documents. However, they introduce concerns relating to accuracy, privacy, accessibility and the protection of stored biometric information.

Verification and identification are different operations

Biometrics may be used for 2 different questions.

OperationQuestion askedComparisonExample
VerificationIs this person the claimed identity holder?1-to-1Comparing a presented fingerprint with the reference linked to a claimed identity.
IdentificationWhich person in a set does this sample correspond to?1-to-manyChecking an enrolment sample against existing records to detect possible duplicates.

In a 1-to-1 comparison, the claimed identity is already known. In a 1-to-many comparison, the system searches multiple reference records for a possible match. In Aadhaar, identifying possible duplicate enrolments and authenticating an existing Aadhaar number holder serve these different purposes.

Biometric matching is not always perfect

A biometric sample can vary because of lighting, position, the quality of the device, changes in the relevant physical characteristic or environmental conditions. Matching systems therefore face the possibility of errors.

  • False acceptance: The system incorrectly accepts a person who should not match the claimed identity.
  • False rejection: The system incorrectly rejects a legitimate person whose sample should match.

These errors have different consequences. False acceptance can create a security risk by permitting impersonation. False rejection can prevent a genuine user from completing a service. The appropriate safeguards depend on the importance of the transaction and the available alternatives.

A failed biometric match does not necessarily establish fraud. The claimant may be genuine, while the sample or matching process may have failed.

Biometrics and exclusion risk

People who perform manual labour may experience worn or damaged fingerprints. Older persons, persons with disabilities and people affected by certain medical conditions may also face difficulties with particular biometric methods. A poorly functioning sensor, unavailable electricity or failed connectivity can interrupt authentication even where the person's identity is not in doubt.

Other permissible methods may therefore be needed, such as an alternative biometric modality, OTP where available, documentary verification or assistance through an authorized service centre. The choice depends on the applicable law and the service's approved procedures.

Privacy and security concerns

Unlike a password, a person's fingerprint or face cannot simply be replaced if related information is compromised. Biometric systems should therefore limit unnecessary collection and disclosure, protect reference information and prevent unauthorized use. A photograph of a face is also not automatically a valid biometric authentication result; a secure system must establish whether the submitted evidence genuinely corresponds to the claimant.

Prelims focus

  • Fingerprint, iris and face are biometric characteristics.
  • Biometric verification is normally a 1-to-1 comparison.
  • Biometric identification may involve a 1-to-many search.
  • Duplicate detection during enrolment is different from later authentication.
  • False acceptance threatens security; false rejection can exclude a genuine user.
  • Trap: A biometric mismatch is not conclusive proof that the claimant is an impostor.

[Sources: Unique Identification Authority of India, 'About Your Aadhaar,' enrolment and de-duplication; UIDAI, 'Authentication,' biometric and face authentication sections; NIST, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, SP 800-63B-4, 2025; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Biometric verification compares against a claimed identity; identification searches multiple records.

title: Biometric Identification: Fingerprints, Iris, Face and Matching Errors

body:
What is Aadhaar?

Aadhaar is a 12-digit random identification number issued by the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) to eligible residents and non-resident Indians holding valid Indian passports after arrival in India, following the prescribed verification and enrolment process. UIDAI is a statutory authority established under the Aadhaar Act, 2016.

Aadhaar is intended to provide a unique, verifiable identity that can be used for appropriate services across India. It is a resident-identification system rather than a register of Indian citizens.

Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016: An Aadhaar number does not confer citizenship or domicile. Aadhaar should therefore not be treated as proof of Indian citizenship.

Information collected during enrolment

Enrolment associates identity information with an individual. UIDAI collects specified demographic details and, where applicable under the enrolment rules, biometric information. Children and certain other categories are subject to special procedures.

CategoryExamples of informationPurpose
DemographicName, date of birth or age, gender, address.Establishing identity details.
Biometric10 fingerprints, 2 iris scans and facial photograph under the standard adult enrolment process.Supporting uniqueness and identity verification.
Contact detailsMobile number and email address, generally optional at enrolment.Enabling relevant communication and services.

For the standard enrolment process, biometric and demographic de-duplication helps identify whether the individual has already been enrolled. This is important because the system aims to issue one Aadhaar number to one individual rather than separate numbers for repeated enrolments.

How Aadhaar authentication works

Authentication occurs when a requesting entity checks a claimed Aadhaar identity through UIDAI's authentication system. Depending on the permitted method, the request may use demographic information, OTP or biometric information. The system compares the submitted information with the relevant record in the Central Identities Data Repository (CIDR).

A basic authentication response may confirm whether the submitted information matches the relevant record. This type of response is different from receiving a full set of personal identity details. The Aadhaar Act provides for authentication responses without disclosing core biometric information to the requesting entity.

Authentication and electronic KYC

In a basic yes-or-no authentication, the requesting service seeks confirmation of a match. In an authorized electronic KYC (e-KYC) process, specified identity information may be supplied in accordance with the applicable rules and consent requirements. e-KYC therefore involves a different information-sharing purpose from a simple match response.

Where Aadhaar can be useful

Aadhaar may support identity verification in government service delivery and other legally permitted contexts. It can reduce the need to submit multiple identity documents where a service accepts appropriate Aadhaar-based verification. The precise requirement depends on the law and service involved.

Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act addresses certain subsidies, benefits and services financed from the Consolidated Fund of India or a State's Consolidated Fund. It permits the relevant government to require authentication or proof of possession of an Aadhaar number, or an application for enrolment if no number has been assigned, while also providing for alternate and viable identification for a person who has not yet been assigned an Aadhaar number.

Aadhaar is not a universal requirement for every activity or service. Whether Aadhaar authentication is mandatory must be determined from the applicable legal provision, not merely from the fact that a service is digital.

Prelims focus

  • UIDAI is the statutory authority responsible for Aadhaar.
  • The Aadhaar Act was enacted in 2016.
  • An Aadhaar number contains 12 digits.
  • Standard adult biometric enrolment includes 10 fingerprints, 2 iris scans and a facial photograph.
  • CIDR means Central Identities Data Repository.
  • Trap: Aadhaar establishes identity under the applicable system; it does not establish citizenship or domicile.

[Sources: UIDAI, 'About Your Aadhaar,' identity features, enrolment and de-duplication; Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016, sections 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12, current amended text published by UIDAI; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]
